title: Handling Imbalanced Data
summary: Training a genuinely good model when the positive class is rare — resampling, class weighting, and threshold moving, done without leaking the test set.

slides.markdown:
Fraud, churn, disease screening — the case you actually care about is often 1% of the data or less. Train naively and a model can hit 99% accuracy by **always predicting the majority class** and never catching a single positive.

Handling imbalance isn't one trick — it's a toolbox: rebalance the data, reweight the loss, or move the decision threshold. Picking the right combination, and evaluating with the right metric, matters more than any single technique.

Most classifiers minimize average loss across all training examples. With 99 negatives for every positive, predicting "negative" every time already gets 99% of the loss right — the optimizer finds little pressure to learn what actually distinguishes the rare positives.

The symptom is a model with high **accuracy** but near-zero **recall** on the class you actually care about. This is why accuracy is the wrong metric here — you need precision/recall, F1, or PR-AUC, which don't reward ignoring the minority class.

slides.subTitle: Oversampling & undersampling
slides.markdown:
Resampling changes the training data's balance directly.

- **Undersampling** — drop majority rows until closer to balanced. Simple, but throws away data and can hurt majority-class performance.
- **Oversampling** — duplicate minority rows, or synthesize new ones. Plain duplication risks overfitting to the same few points.
- **SMOTE** — generates new minority points by interpolating between a real one and its nearest minority neighbors, more variety than duplication.

All three only touch the training set — never validation or test data.

Instead of touching the data, **class weighting** touches the loss function: mistakes on the minority class are multiplied by a larger weight (often the inverse of class frequency), so the optimizer is penalized harder for missing them.

This achieves a similar effect to oversampling without physically duplicating or synthesizing rows — useful when you want to avoid inflating dataset size or when using a model (like `class_weight='balanced'` in scikit-learn) that supports it natively. It's often the cheapest first thing to try.

A model trained normally still outputs a usable probability — the imbalance mainly biases the **default 0.5 threshold**, not the ranking of predictions. **Threshold moving** picks a different cutoff (e.g. flag anything above 0.1 as positive) chosen from the precision/recall trade-off you actually need.

This is often the cheapest fix of all: no retraining required, just sweep thresholds against a validation set and pick the one hitting your target recall or precision. It composes well with resampling or weighting rather than replacing them.

Three tools, different situations.

| Approach | Cost | Best when |
|---|---|---|
| Resampling (SMOTE) | Retrain, more data prep | Moderate imbalance, enough minority examples |
| Class weighting | Retrain, no data change | Model supports it; want to avoid synthetic rows |
| Threshold moving | No retraining | Model already ranks well; just need the right cutoff |
| Anomaly detection | Different model family | Extreme imbalance (<0.1%), positives look like outliers |

At extreme rarity, framing it as **anomaly detection** (model "normal" and flag deviations) can beat any classifier — there's barely enough positives to learn a class boundary from at all.

**The mistake:** applying SMOTE to the **whole dataset** before splitting into train and test.

**Why it breaks:** SMOTE synthesizes new minority points by interpolating between real ones. If that happens before the split, a synthetic training point can be interpolated from real minority points that ended up in the test set — the model effectively gets a sneak peek at test data, inflating validation metrics that won't hold up in production.

**The fix:** always split first, then apply SMOTE **only to the training fold** — test data must stay untouched and unseen.

slides.subTitle: Setting a threshold from real cost numbers
slides.markdown:
Say catching a fraud case saves $200, and a false positive (flagging a legitimate transaction) costs $10 in customer friction and review time. If a threshold of 0.3 catches 80 fraud cases and generates 400 false positives per day, the trade is `80 * $200 = $16,000` saved against `400 * $10 = $4,000` cost — clearly worth it. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 might catch 90 fraud cases (`$18,000` saved) but generate 2,000 false positives (`$20,000` cost) — now net negative.

This is threshold moving (s05) made concrete: instead of picking a threshold that "looks reasonable" on a PR curve, compute the expected cost at each candidate threshold using your actual per-error costs, and pick the one that minimizes total expected cost, not the one that maximizes an abstract metric like F1.

slides.subTitle: Non-stratified cross-validation can starve a fold of positives
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A standard random k-fold split works the same way regardless of class balance."

**Why it's wrong:** with a rare positive class, a plain random split can by chance put very few — or even zero — positive examples in some folds. A fold with no positives can't compute precision/recall/F1 meaningfully at all, and one with unusually few produces a wildly noisy per-fold metric, making your cross-validation score unstable and hard to trust.

**Correct model:** always use **stratified** k-fold splitting for imbalanced problems (scikit-learn's `StratifiedKFold`), which preserves each fold's class ratio close to the overall dataset's — a small change that prevents an entire category of noisy, misleading validation results.
